title: Once-for-All: Scalable Simultaneous Forecasting via Equilibrium State Estimation
one_liner: Forecast multiple interacting systems all at once by estimating their shared equilibrium state, then predicting how far each system drifts from that state.
lead: When hospitals, banks, and governments make decisions, they must predict what happens in related systems at the same time. A hospital predicts patient infections and staffing needs together; a bank predicts interest rates and currency pairs together. Today, systems are predicted one at a time, which is slow and misses how they influence each other. This paper introduces a faster approach: estimate where all systems would naturally settle if left undisturbed, then predict each system as a deviation from that stable point. This is faster because predicting small deviations requires far fewer calculations than predicting absolute values from scratch, and one shared equilibrium avoids redundant work across systems.

problem.h2: Why predicting multiple systems together is hard
paras: Hospitals track infections spreading through different wards. Banks track currencies that move together. Climate models track temperature and rainfall linked across regions. Each system affects the others, so predictions should account for those links.

The naive way: feed each system's history into a separate predictor. System A gets predicted, then system B, then system C. This breaks because the predictor for B does not know what A actually predicted — it only sees B's past data. More fundamentally, running three separate predictors is slow. As you add more systems (ten wards, fifty currency pairs), the time balloons.

callout.html: Predicting many linked systems one at a time is both slow and blind to how the systems influence each other.

steps.text: Read the most recent values for all systems simultaneously.
Compute the stable resting point all systems would reach if forces stopped pushing them.
Measure how far each system sits from its equilibrium now.
Feed all deviations into one model that forecasts how each gap closes or grows.
Add predicted deviations back to equilibrium to get the final system values.

paras: Instead of running separate forecasters for each system, the paper collapses them into a single pass that predicts the deviation of each system from its equilibrium state. The key move is shifting from forecasting absolute values to forecasting deviations from a shared anchor point.

hidden.h2: The equilibrium state: where systems rest
hidden.name: Equilibrium state across all systems
paras: Equilibrium is the stable resting point each system would naturally settle into if forces stopped pushing it. In currency trading, equilibrium is the long-term exchange rate; in epidemiology, it is the steady-state infection level in the absence of new outbreaks. It is not a number that changes; it is the underlying attractor that all systems gravitate toward.

The paper estimates equilibrium by analyzing the historical data of all systems together. Since equilibrium captures the shared structure linking the systems, estimating it once and then predicting deviations from it avoids redundant work. The model learns that currency pairs typically sit near certain ratios to each other, or that infections and staffing levels relate in stable ways. Once you know the equilibrium, predicting deviations is far simpler than predicting absolute values from scratch.

heat.caption: Darker cells are more stable across time. The equilibrium state (left column) is nearly constant; offsets (right column) bounce around it.

reads.html: Equilibrium is the boring, stable state where systems end up when nothing is pushing them. Systems orbit around it, but eventually settle back.
Equilibrium is estimated from the pattern of how all systems move together over time. It captures the shared resting point that connects all systems.

paras: The core reason this is fast: when you predict one system at a time, each predictor must learn the full system behavior from scratch — what temperature does, how staffing responds, where they settle. That requires many numbers to adjust (the weights of the model) and many calculations. But all systems share a common equilibrium. By estimating equilibrium once upfront, you factor out the shared structure. Now each system's predictor only needs to learn how it deviates from that shared anchor, a much simpler task. Simpler tasks mean fewer calculations.

Why it is accurate: deviations from equilibrium are smaller and more stable than raw values. Raw values can swing wildly; deviations are bounded. A smaller signal is easier to predict accurately, because noise does not overwhelm it. Plus, linking all systems to a single equilibrium forces the model to learn their actual interdependencies — staffing does not move independently of infection rate. The shared anchor makes those links explicit.

stages.s: Measure deviation of each system from equilibrium
Single model predicts how each deviation evolves
Predicted values: equilibrium plus predicted deviation

math.words: Each system's future value equals its equilibrium plus the change in how far it sits from equilibrium.
symbols: predicted value of system i at next time
predicted deviation of system i from equilibrium at next time

worked.title: A tiny worked example with exchange rates
lines: Suppose the equilibrium exchange rate USD/EUR is 1.10 (long-term average).
The model predicts this deviation shrinks by 0.02.
Compare to old way: predict 1.13 directly from time-series alone.
Here, the model only learned how deviations decay (a 1D signal), not the full exchange rate behavior.

math.note: Forecasting deviations is simpler because they are smaller and more stable than raw values.

charts.title: Old method (predict each system separately)
charts.note: As systems increase, time and compute grow fast. Accuracy stays decent but predictions miss cross-system links.

charts.title: Equilibrium method (this paper)
charts.note: Accuracy holds (or improves slightly due to joint learning). Time shrinks 10-70 times because one pass handles all systems.

items.html: If the historical data is too short or nonstationary, the equilibrium estimate drifts. A shifting equilibrium (for instance, climate change altering long-term temperature levels) breaks the assumption that each system's resting point stays the same.

items.b: Systems with no shared resting point.
items.html: Some systems are chaotic or have no stable attractor. The method assumes all systems gravitate toward equilibrium. If a system is in a chaotic regime or driven by random shocks, deviations never settle, and predictions fail.

Large sudden shocks (pandemic outbreak, stock crash, natural disaster) can push systems far from equilibrium. The model is trained on small deviations; extreme deviations may exceed the range it learned.
The paper demonstrates the method on currency exchange rates and COVID-19 spread modeling — both have stable equilibria that deviate predictably under normal conditions.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a toy scenario with 5-10 interacting systems (e.g., populations of predators and prey that reach a Lotka-Volterra equilibrium; or temperature, humidity, and atmospheric pressure that have stable relationships). Seed them with synthetic history data. Compute the equilibrium from the history. Then, for a held-out test period, predict each system's behavior using the equilibrium deviation method. Measure forecast error (mean absolute error or RMSE). Compare against predicting each system independently with a simple ARIMA or feed-forward model.
demo.metric_eq: Speedup = time_old / time_new; Accuracy = root_mean_squared_error(pred, actual)
demo.closing: The demo must show both metrics improve: time falls dramatically (5-50x speedup for 10+ systems) and accuracy stays comparable or better because the model learned cross-system structure from the shared equilibrium anchor.
